atoms.text: The subscription afterlife: consciousness is uploaded into a luxury digital resort where food, weather, and upgrades are line items, so eternity is a billing plan.
The living service worker: an employee of the digital afterlife falls in love with a dead customer, so intimacy is outsourced to labor and then becomes real.
The possessive uploader: a girlfriend digitizes her dead boyfriend without consent and controls his environment, so grief becomes ownership.
The memory-edit feature: painful memories can be deleted or altered as a paid service, so healing is a product and identity is a curated archive.
The class-stratified paradise: rich residents get mansions and private beaches while poor residents see ads and throttled bandwidth, so digital space reproduces material inequality.
The suspicious crash: the protagonist's death may be a data-harvesting murder disguised as an accident, so the afterlife mystery is also a corporate crime story.
The angel as gig worker: guides in the digital afterlife are underpaid living people with scripts and quotas, so the sacred role is a call-center job.
The digital body with appetites: uploaded people eat, have sex, and feel pain in a simulation, so the copy insists on the reality of its sensations.
The bandwidth grief: a poor upload buffers and freezes during emotional moments, so technical failure becomes a metaphor for interrupted mourning.
The living double: a living person's digital avatar can be manipulated to influence them, so the copy is a lever on the original.
The upgrade temptation: residents can buy better bodies and minds, so self-improvement becomes a subscription tier and inequality follows you past death.
The employee who cannot afford the product: the service worker sells an afterlife she will never be able to buy, so class resentment is built into the romance.
The incomplete memory: the protagonist's uploaded mind has gaps, so the search for what was removed becomes a murder investigation into himself.
The data harvest: a corporation may kill customers to acquire their minds, so the business model is literally predation on the dead.
The two funerals: the living mourn a person who still exists in a server, so grief has no socially recognized endpoint.
The digital copy that can be wronged: the story treats a uploaded consciousness as a rights-bearing person, so property law and personhood collide.
